messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus's Story

Marcus was seventeen when the tornado touched down outside Omaha. He'd been working his shift at the Burger King on Highway 275 when the manager shouted to get everyone away from the windows. He remembered the sound first—a roar like nothing he'd ever heard, a freight train amplified a thousand times, filling his chest with a vibration he could feel in his teeth. The lights had flickered once, twice, then died. In the darkness, he'd crouched with three coworkers in the walk-in freezer, listening to the building scream around them. When they finally emerged, the restaurant was gutted. The roof was gone. The smell—wet concrete, torn insulation, something chemical and acrid—had filled his lungs, and even now, nineteen months later, when Marcus closed his eyes and let himself think about that day, he could taste it at the back of his throat.

The physical injuries had healed within weeks. A fractured wrist, some lacerations. But something else had fractured too, something Marcus couldn't see in a mirror or wrap in a cast. For months afterward, he'd tried to push through it. He'd returned to work within two weeks, convinced that showing up, staying normal, would prove the tornado hadn't changed him. But the more he tried to move forward, the more he became convinced that he couldn't—that whatever person he'd been before that freezer was gone for good. The realization had crept up on him slowly. He used to joke around with coworkers, used to look forward to things. Now he felt hollowed out, a shell of someone else's life. He had become unrecognizable to himself, and the thought terrified him in a way that made no sense, because it was his own mind doing the recognizing.

When memories of the tornado surfaced—and they did, unbidden, at random moments—they came with the full force of the original terror. A car alarm in the parking lot would trigger a flash of the freezer darkness. The smell of the industrial kitchen would suddenly morph into that acrid chemical stench, and his body would respond as though the danger were happening again, right then, his heart hammering, his breath shallow. The images were vivid and intrusive: the manager's face in the moment before they ran, the texture of the metal shelving he'd gripped. These memories weren't like normal remembering; they felt like reliving, complete with the same suffocating dread he'd felt trapped in that freezer. Because he'd come to believe that he was fundamentally and permanently damaged, that the tornado had rewired something essential in him, every intrusive memory felt like confirmation. Each time the terror returned, it reinforced his conviction that he was broken now, that this was his new reality.

Desperate to escape the thoughts and the memories and the unbearable feeling of being someone he didn't recognize, Marcus had begun to construct barriers around himself. Before any conversation—with a customer, a coworker, his mother—he would rehearse what he might say, running through possible exchanges in his head like a script, trying to anticipate what might go wrong and how he might control it. He avoided anything that felt remotely stressful: he'd stopped going to his friend Diego's house because the drive took him past the highway where the tornado had touched down; he'd declined his cousin's wedding invitation because crowds felt overwhelming; he'd even started taking shifts at the quietest times, avoiding the busy lunch rush. And whenever the thoughts came—the images, the smells, the creeping certainty that he was irreparably changed—he would try with all his strength not to think about them, pushing them away, distracting himself with his phone or his work, anything to keep the memories at bay.

But the avoidance had a cost he hadn't anticipated. By rehearsing conversations and controlling every interaction, by shrinking his world to only the safest scenarios, Marcus had reinforced his own sense that he couldn't handle normal life anymore—that the world was too dangerous and he was too fragile. His attempts to suppress the thoughts often backfired; the harder he pushed them away, the more forcefully they returned. And his growing isolation, the way he'd withdrawn from people and places, had left him with fewer ways to challenge the belief that he was permanently damaged. He'd missed Diego's birthday dinner. His mother had stopped asking him to family events. Two months ago, his manager had asked if he was okay, and Marcus had said nothing, just shrugged and gone back to the register. He wasn't okay. He was nineteen years old and felt like a stranger in his own skin, and the person he used to be—the one who could laugh, who had plans, who wasn't afraid all the time—felt like someone he'd read about in a story, not someone he'd ever actually been.

It was his mother who finally insisted he talk to someone. Marcus had resisted, convinced that therapy wouldn't help someone as broken as he was, but he'd come to the appointment anyway, still rehearsing what he might say, still braced for the moment when his own mind would betray him again with an image or a smell or that terrible sense of falling that had no bottom.
